archetype.name: Pretender (overtime-fueled)
archetype.definition: San Jose's record sits ahead of its play: every win has come past regulation while it gets badly out-chanced at 5-on-5, so the standings flatter a team whose underlying numbers sit near the league's bottom.

report.headline: Four overtime wins mask a team getting buried at 5-on-5
report.take:
The Sharks sit 4-3-1 and on pace for 92 standings points, which looks like real progress from a franchise that finished last in 2024-25 and climbed to 86 points last year. Look at how the wins arrived, though. Florida 4-3, Los Angeles 5-4, St. Louis 3-2 and Nashville 3-2 all went past regulation, and nothing in regulation has gone San Jose's way. Their Pts vs Goal Diff of 2.2 ranks first in the league, while the goal differential of -9 ranks 27th per game and paces out to -82 over a full season. The record is the noise. The differential is the signal.

The 5-on-5 game is the real worry. An xGF % of .408 ranks 29th, more than nine points below the league's even split. Of the regulars, only Macklin Celebrini (.503) is breaking even on expected goals. The blueline is uniformly underwater: Darnell Nurse and Luca Cagnoni both sit around .35. Shot volume is roughly league average both ways, so the problem is shot quality, not puck possession. That shows up in a CF % of .48 that is merely below par next to an xGF % that is near the bottom.

The numbers also hide some luck running the other way. A 5-on-5 PDO of 94.5 and a 9.5% team shooting rate, 25th in the league, say the finishing has been cold, and some of that will come back. The goaltending split matters just as much. Alex Nedeljkovic has a .920 save percentage and +4.2 GSAx in three starts, while Yaroslav Askarov sits at .848 and -2.0 in five. That gap, not the team's structure, is why the Goalies GSAx lands at a league-average 2.1.

This follows a pattern. Last season San Jose banked 6.1 points over its goal differential on a .476 xGF %. This year's chance share is worse, and overtime luck rarely carries a team two years running. The 1-3-1 last five games, at 2.2 goals a game, are what the floor looks like when the coin flips stop landing.

strengths.title: Celebrini drives everything that works
strengths.body: Celebrini has 11 points in six games and 6 power-play points, and he ranks 16th on the centers tab. He is the only forward winning his minutes on expected goals. That is a sustainable, talent-driven profile. The catch is how much the offense depends on him: no other forward has more than 6 points.

strengths.title: Power play above league average
strengths.body: A 23.1% power play ranks 11th, well above the league's 20.4%. Ivar Stenberg has 5 PP points alongside Celebrini, so the unit has more than one finisher. Because it leans on top-end skill rather than bounces, it should hold up reasonably well.

strengths.title: Nedeljkovic giving them a chance
strengths.body: In three starts Nedeljkovic has stopped .920 with +4.2 GSAx and ranks 14th on the goalies tab. That kind of netminding keeps a poor-chance team in close games. Three starts is a tiny sample, but it gives the coaching staff a clear alternative to Askarov's start.

concerns.title: Outchanced badly at even strength
concerns.body: A .408 xGF % ranks 29th, and nearly every regular skater is below .45. Michael Misa (.299) and Stenberg (.337) are being swamped. This is structural rather than bad luck, and it is worse than last season's already weak .476.

concerns.title: Overtime luck propping up the record
concerns.body: The Sharks rank first in Pts vs Goal Diff, and all four wins needed extra time. The goal differential ranks 27th per game, which is the profile of a much worse record. Close-game luck regresses, and the standings points will drift down toward the margin.

concerns.title: Askarov's rough start in net
concerns.body: Askarov has made the most starts but owns an .848 save percentage and -2.0 GSAx. That drags the team's all-situations save percentage to 24th. If he keeps getting the bulk of the work at this level, the defensive shortcomings get punished every night.

trend.note: An opening run of overtime wins has given way to a 1-3-1 stretch over the last five games, with scoring down to 2.2 a game. The results are catching up to the chance numbers.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games, including Boston, before Buffalo's leaky penalty kill
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with three straight road games against Montréal, Ottawa and Boston, then Buffalo at home. Montréal and Buffalo both have poor goaltending: the Canadiens' .868 save percentage ranks 28th and the Sabres' .861 ranks 30th. Both also leak points to forwards. The problem is that both out-chance their opponents, Montréal at a .543 xGF % and Buffalo at .525, so San Jose's 5-on-5 weakness won't get a break.

Boston is the clear outlier. The Bruins are second on the site, grade A in every group, and already beat the Sharks 6-3 on October 13. Their 107.8 all-situations PDO says some of that is running hot, but they will still be heavy favorites. Ottawa scores little, ranking 29th in shots for per game, and could produce a low-event game. The Senators' A- goaltending and their stinginess toward centers aim straight at San Jose's best players.

keyMatchups.title: Sharks power play vs Buffalo's kill
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo kills only 64.5% of penalties, 30th in the league, and its goalies are 30th in save percentage. San Jose's 23.1% power play is its most reliable source of offense. The home finale is where the special-teams edge should turn into goals.

keyMatchups.title: Ottawa's stinginess toward centers
keyMatchups.body: The Senators rank 6th at holding centers under their expected points. San Jose's offense runs through Celebrini and Will Smith at center. Ottawa's wingers rank 27th by the same measure, so production may have to come from the flanks.

keyMatchups.title: Boston's hot-running juggernaut
keyMatchups.body: Boston has a +1.67 goal differential per game, second in the league, and an all-situations PDO of 107.8. Some of that shooting will cool, but its A grades across forwards, defense and goal are a hard matchup for a team at a .408 xGF %.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net, and whether Nedeljkovic's form earns him the bulk of a road-heavy week.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the record to slide toward the goal differential. The overtime luck that leads the league is the least repeatable part of the profile, and the .408 xGF % suggests the true talent is a bottom-eight team at 5-on-5. Two things push back. Cold finishing (9.5% shooting, 94.5 PDO) should warm up, and Celebrini plus a top-half power play give the offense a real engine. Goaltending is the swing: if Nedeljkovic's level holds and he takes more starts, San Jose can stay in the low-80s points range of last year. If Askarov's start continues, it falls further.

Our range is roughly 31 to 37 wins and 72 to 84 standings points, well short of the 92-point pace. Goal differential per game should improve from its current depth as shooting normalizes, but it should still finish in the bottom third of the league.
swingFactors: Goaltending split between Nedeljkovic and Askarov
Whether 5-on-5 chance share climbs off the bottom tier

confidence.note: Only eight or nine games played, but the luck and chance-share signals all point the same way.
